canonical_concept.beeja: ह्रीं (Hrīm) — the bīja of Prakṛti as the creative power. Also क्लीं (Klīm) — the bīja of attraction and manifestation.
canonical_concept.vyakarana: Prakṛti is a feminine noun derived from the prefix pra- and the root kṛ (to make) with the suffix -ti. The feminine gender is significant — Prakṛti is the feminine creative principle, complementary to the masculine Puruṣa.
canonical_concept.functional_meaning: Prakṛti is the primal, undifferentiated matter from which the entire manifest universe evolves. In Sāṃkhya philosophy, Prakṛti consists of three guṇas (qualities): Sattva (clarity, luminosity), Rajas (activity, passion), Tamas (inertia, darkness). When the three guṇas are in perfect equilibrium, Prakṛti is unmanifest (avyakta). When the equilibrium is disturbed (by Puruṣa's proximity), Prakṛti begins to evolve the universe through twenty-three tattvas (principles).
canonical_concept.dhatu: प्र + कृ (Pra + Kṛ) — Pra (before, primary, forth) + Kṛ (to do, to make). The primary maker; the original nature; that which was made first.
canonical_concept.nirukta: "Prakṛṣṭā kṛtiḥ prakṛtiḥ" — the primary creation. Prakṛti is the original nature from which all manifest existence emerges.
canonical_concept.tattva: Prakṛti-Tattva — the principle of primal matter and creative nature. In Sāṃkhya: Prakṛti is one of the two ultimate realities (along with Puruṣa). It is the material cause of the universe — the primal matter from which all manifest existence evolves.

claims.value: In Sāṃkhya: Prakṛti is one of the two ultimate realities — it is the material cause of the universe. It is unconscious (acetana) but active. Puruṣa is conscious but inactive. The universe is the product of their interaction. In Advaita: Prakṛti = Māyā — the creative power of Brahman. In Viśiṣṭādvaita: Prakṛti is the body of Brahman-Viṣṇu — real and dependent on Brahman. In Śākta: Prakṛti = the Goddess — the supreme creative reality.

claims.value: In Sāṃkhya cosmology: from Prakṛti evolves Mahat (cosmic intellect), then Ahaṃkāra (ego-principle), then the five tanmātras (subtle elements), then the five mahābhūtas (gross elements), then the ten indriyas (sense and action organs), then manas (mind) — twenty-three tattvas in total. The universe is Prakṛti's evolution for Puruṣa's experience and eventual liberation.

claims.value: Prakṛti as psychological principle: the three guṇas govern all psychological states. Sattva produces clarity, wisdom, and peace. Rajas produces activity, desire, and restlessness. Tamas produces inertia, delusion, and sleep. The goal of yoga is to transcend all three guṇas (triguṇātīta) and rest in Puruṣa's pure consciousness.

claims.value: The concept of Prakṛti in governance: the Arthaśāstra describes the seven elements of the state (saptāṅga) as the Prakṛti of the kingdom — king, minister, territory, fort, treasury, army, ally. The concept of rāja-prakṛti (the nature of the king) — the king's guṇa-composition determines the quality of governance.

claims.value: In Āyurveda: Prakṛti is the individual's constitutional nature — the unique combination of the three doṣas (vāta, pitta, kapha) determined at conception. The concept of deha-prakṛti (body-nature) — each person has a unique Prakṛti that determines their health tendencies. Āyurvedic treatment is tailored to the individual's Prakṛti.

claims.value: The concept of Prakṛti in mathematics: the three guṇas as the three fundamental operations (addition/sattva, multiplication/rajas, subtraction/tamas). The concept of Prakṛti in Bījaganita (algebra) — the term prakṛti is used for the coefficient in quadratic equations.

claims.value: The concept of Prakṛti in ritual: the three guṇas determine the nature of ritual offerings. Sattvic offerings (milk, ghee, fruits) are for liberation. Rajasic offerings (meat, wine) are for worldly power. Tamasic offerings are for destructive purposes. The Bhagavad Gītā (17.7-10) describes the three types of food, sacrifice, and worship according to the three guṇas.
